## Warm Up {.activity}

Describe each set in words, and in set-builder notation if you can.

::::: columns
::: {.column}
1. $\{x\in\mathbb{Z} : 3 \mid x\} \cap \{x\in\mathbb{Z} : 2 \mid x\}$
2. $\{x\in\mathbb{Z} : 4 \mid x\} \cap \{x\in\mathbb{Z} : 6 \mid x\}$
3. $\{x\in\mathbb{Z} : 3 \mid x\} \cap \{x\in\mathbb{Z} : 9 \mid x\}$
:::
::: {.column}
4. $\{x\in\mathbb{Z} : 3 \mid x\} \cup \{x\in\mathbb{Z} : 9 \mid x\}$
5. $\{x\in\mathbb{Z} : 3 \mid x\} \cup \{x\in\mathbb{Z} : 2 \mid x\}$. Is it the multiples of anything?
:::
:::::

::: notes
1. Multiples of 6.
2. Multiples of 12, not 24: 12 is the smallest number both 4 and 6 divide.
3. Multiples of 9. Every multiple of 9 is a multiple of 3, so intersecting
   with the multiples of 3 removes nothing.
4. Multiples of 3. Adding the multiples of 9 adds nothing new.
5. No. It contains 2 and 3, so it could only be the multiples of 1, but it
   doesn't contain 5. Unions of "multiples of" sets usually aren't one.
3 and 4 lead into the proofs: if B is a subset of A, then A n B = B and
A u B = A.
:::

# Set Proofs

## Setup {.smaller}

**We’ll use these café sets:**

$I$ = "iced orders" ( `df['is_iced']`)

$N$ = "non-dairy milk" (`df['milk']=='Oat' | df['milk'] == 'Almond'`)

$O$ = "oat-milk orders" (`df['milk'] == 'Oat'`)

$A$ = "almond-milk orders" (`df['milk'] == 'Almond'`)

$H$ = "high-caffeine" (`df['caffeine_mg'] >= 150`)

$L$ = "low-calorie" (`df['calories'] <= 150`)

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/UBC-CS/dsci220/refs/heads/main/data/cafe_orders.csv')

I = df['is_iced']
N = df['milk'].str.strip().isin(['Oat','Almond'])
O = df['milk'].str.strip().eq('Oat')
H = df['caffeine_mg'] >= 150
```

## Partition Identity {.smaller}

**Story:** Split **iced** orders by whether they’re **non-dairy** ($N$) or **not** ($N^c$). We should neither lose nor double-count any iced orders.

**Theorem:** For any sets $I$ and $N$,
$$
(I\cap N)\ \cup\ (I\cap N^{c}) \;=\; I
\quad\text{and}\quad
(I\cap N)\ \cap\ (I\cap N^{c}) \;=\; \varnothing.
$$

**Apply:**  

* Because the union is "disjoint",
$|I| \;=\; |I\cap N| \;+\; |I\cap N^c|$
* This is the basis for the "Law of Total Probability," which you will see someday!

```{pyodide}
# Sanity check on your data:
left  = (I & N).sum() + (I & ~N).sum()
right = I.sum()
disjoint = ((I & N) & (I & ~N)).sum()
left, right, disjoint, (left == right)  
```

## Partition Identity Proof {.smaller}

**Theorem:** For any sets $I$ and $N$,
$$
(I\cap N)\ \cup\ (I\cap N^{c}) \;=\; I
\quad\text{and}\quad
(I\cap N)\ \cap\ (I\cap N^{c}) \;=\; \varnothing.
$$

**Proof:**  

::: notes
Consider arbitrary sets I and N.
Union, two subsets.
(subset) Let x be in (I n N) u (I n N^c). Then x is in I n N or in I n N^c;
in either case x is in I.
(superset) Let x be in I. By cases on x and N: if x is in N, then x is in
I n N; if not, x is in N^c, so x is in I n N^c. Either way x is in the union.
Intersection. Suppose some x is in both I n N and I n N^c. Then x is in N
and x is in N^c, i.e. x is in N and x is not in N -- a contradiction. So no
x is in both: the intersection is the empty set. (Empty set is a subset of
everything, so showing nothing is in it is the whole job.)
Techniques: element-chasing for =, proof by cases (in N or not -- excluded
middle), proof by contradiction for "= empty set".
:::

## Partition Identity Proof: Nothing in Both {.smaller}

The **empty set** $\varnothing$ is the set with no elements. To show a set is
$\varnothing$, we show that nothing is in it.

**Claim:** $(I\cap N)\ \cap\ (I\cap N^{c}) = \varnothing$.

**Proof** (by contradiction)**:** Suppose some $x$ is in both $I\cap N$ and
$I\cap N^c$.

* Since $x\in I\cap N$, we have $x\in N$.
* Since $x\in I\cap N^c$, we have $x\in N^c$, so $x\notin N$.

So $x\in N$ and $x\notin N$, which is a contradiction. No $x$ is in both, and
the intersection is $\varnothing$. $\blacksquare$

In code, this is a mask that selects nobody: `((I & N) & (I & ~N)).sum()` is
always 0.

## Complement Flips the Order, by Contradiction {.smaller}

**Theorem:** If $O\subseteq N$, then $N^{c}\subseteq O^{c}$.

**Proof** (by contradiction)**:** Suppose $O\subseteq N$. Consider an arbitrary
$x\in N^c$, so $x\notin N$. We show $x\in O^c$.

. . .

Suppose, for contradiction, that $x\notin O^c$. Then $x\in O$.

. . .

Since $O\subseteq N$ and $x\in O$, we have $x\in N$.

. . .

So $x\in N$ and $x\notin N$, which is a contradiction. Hence $x\in O^c$, and
$N^c\subseteq O^c$. $\blacksquare$

. . .

Compare: the contrapositive of $x\in O\rightarrow x\in N$ is
$x\notin N\rightarrow x\notin O$, which is the whole theorem in one line.

```{pyodide}
(~N & O).sum()   # should be 0 if N^c ⊆ O^c (equivalently, no row is ~N AND O)
```

# Regular Expressions

## Regular Expressions: Languages and Filters

Goals:

* See a regex as a set descriptor (a language over an alphabet).

* Read/write the core regex operators.

* Use regex to filter rows in a DataFrame: `df['col'].str.contains(pattern)`.

* Tell the two apart: a **language** is a set of strings; a **filter** gives a set of rows.

::: notes
Bridge from sets: a subset is just a predicate. Regex gives us predicates on strings.
:::

## From Sets to Strings {.smaller}

Sets: $A=\{x\in U: P(x)\}$

\

A regular expression $r$ does two different jobs.

* **Language.** $L(r)=\{w\in\Sigma^*: \text{the whole of } w \text{ matches } r\}$.
  A set of _strings_, usually infinite.
  In Python: `re.fullmatch(r, w)`. In pandas: `df['col'].str.fullmatch(r)`.

* **Filter.** Keep the rows whose string has _some part_ that matches $r$.
  A set of _rows_, a subset of the dataframe.
  In pandas: `df['col'].str.contains(r)`.

\

Today: languages first, then filters.

## Warm-Up: In or Out? {.activity}

`pattern = [A-Z]{2}\d{3}`
$L = L($`pattern`$)$, so the whole string must match.

\ 

Which strings are in the set $L$?

\ 

`CS110`

`ab123`

`DS2200`

`MA101`

\

::: notes
This pattern says: 2 capital letters, then 3 digits, and nothing else.
In: CS110, MA101. Out: ab123 (lower case), DS2200 (four digits).
Save DS2200: as a filter, contains keeps it, because DS220 is a part of it.
:::

## Standard Operators {.smaller}

Literals: `cat`

Dot: `.` any char (except newline)

Class: `[aeiou]` or ranges like `[A-Z0-9]`

Negated class: `[^,]` anything but comma

Alternation: `(cat|dog)`

Quantifiers: `a*` 0 or more, `a+` or more, `a?` 0 or 1, `{m,n}` range

Anchors (filters only): `^` start, `$` end

Escapes: `\.` literal dot

Groups: `(  )` captures, `(?:  )` non-capturing


## Regex vs. Language {.smaller}

Fix an alphabet of characters, $\Sigma$.

Then a pattern $r$ denotes the language $L(r)=\{w\in\Sigma^*: \text{the whole of } w \text{ matches } r\}$

* if no string matches the pattern,  $L=\varnothing$

* the empty pattern matches only the empty string ⇒ $L=\{\varepsilon\}$

* pattern `a` means $L=\{$`a`$\}$

* Concatenated patterns `AB` means $L(A)L(B)=\{xy:x\in L(A),y\in L(B)\}$

* Union of patterns: `A|B` means $L(A)\cup L(B)$

* Kleene Star: `A*` means all finite concatenations from $L(A)$ (incl. $\varepsilon$)

::: notes
Same spirit as set algebra: union / product / closure.
No anchors here: a language always means the whole string.
:::

## Say the Set 

\ 

`(ab|ba)*`: strings over `{a,b}` that are concatenations of `ab` or `ba`.

\

`(0|1)*11(0|1)*`: all binary strings containing 11 as a substring.

\

`1(01|10)*0`: binary strings that start with 1, end with 0, and are filled with `{0,1}` pairs that flip from `1` to `0` or vice versa.

## Same Pattern, Two Jobs {.smaller}

`pattern = 'Latte'`, so $L($`pattern`$)=\{$`Latte`$\}$. How many café orders does each line keep? Predict, then run.

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/UBC-CS/dsci220/refs/heads/main/data/cafe_orders.csv')

pattern = 'Latte'
print(df['drink'].str.fullmatch(pattern).sum())   # whole string is in L
print(df['drink'].str.match(pattern).sum())       # string starts with something in L
print(df['drink'].str.contains(pattern).sum())    # some part of the string is in L
```

. . .

* `fullmatch` is **membership** in $L$: only `Latte` itself.
* `contains` is a **filter**: it also keeps `Iced Latte`, `Chai Latte`, `Matcha Latte`.
  Those strings are not in $L$. They are in $\Sigma^* L\, \Sigma^*$, the strings with a part in $L$.
* Anchors turn a filter back into membership: `contains('^Latte$')` keeps the same rows as `fullmatch('Latte')`.

::: notes
Counts: 2, 2, 5. Try pattern = 'Iced' too: 0, 2, 2.
The DS2200 callback from the warm-up: not in L, but contains keeps it.
:::


## Back to the Cafe

Suppose a column `drink` has values like:
<span class="rule">"Iced Latte", "Drip Coffee", "Americano", "Chai Latte", "Tea", "Espresso"</span>

\ 

Goals:

1. Keep espresso-style drinks: "espresso", "americano", "latte", or "cappuccino"

2. "Iced" appears as a whole word

3. Drinks that end with “Tea”

## Cafe continued

```{pyodide}
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/UBC-CS/dsci220/refs/heads/main/data/cafe_orders.csv')

# regex
esprestr = r'(?i)\b(espresso|americano|latte|cappuccino)\b'
icedrestr = r'(?i)\biced\b'
tearestr = r'(?i)tea$'

# masks
espressoish = df['drink'].str.contains(esprestr, regex=True, na=False)
iced       = df['drink'].str.contains(icedrestr, regex=True, na=False)
teas       = df['drink'].str.contains(tearestr,  regex=True, na=False)

# Set algebra on masks:
E_or_I   = espressoish | iced          # union
I_and_T  = iced & teas                 # intersection
not_I    = ~iced                       # complement

# Project the data:
subset = df[E_or_I]
subset
```

## Typical Patterns


Whole word: <span class="rule">r'\\biced\\b'</span>

Starts with: <span class="rule">r'^Iced'</span>

Ends with: <span class="rule">r'Tea$'</span>

Optional word: <span class="rule">r'^(Iced )?Latte$'</span>

One of set (case-insensitive):  

<center>
<span class="rule"> r'(?i)\\b(espresso|americano|latte|cappuccino)\\b'</span>
</center>

## Reminder: From Filter to Language {.smaller}

Let $\Sigma$ = letters, numbers, and spaces.

Pattern <span class="rule">(?i)(espresso|americano|latte|cappuccino)</span> denotes a language $L\subseteq \Sigma^*$.

This parallels:

Set: $L=\{\,w\in\Sigma^*: \text{the whole of } w \text{ matches the pattern}\,\}$

Predicate: $P(w)=\texttt{fullmatch}(\text{pattern}, w)$

Mask: <span class="rule">df['drink'].str.fullmatch(pattern)</span>

\

A filter with <span class="rule">str.contains(pattern)</span> is a membership test too, for a
bigger language: $\Sigma^* L\, \Sigma^*$, the strings that have a part in $L$.

You’ve been doing language membership tests all class, with filters.
